ASK:
What does a load factor of 1g mean in level flight?
ANSWER: When the wing produces lift equal to the airplane’s weight, the aircraft is in level flight. This results in a load factor of 1g, meaning the lift force is directly opposing gravity.

Why must lift increase during a banked turn to maintain altitude?
ANSWER: In a banked turn, part of the lift is redirected horizontally to turn the aircraft. To maintain altitude, the total lift must increase to counteract gravity. This increase depends on the bank angle, which raises the load factor above 1g.

Pilots are normally reluctant to reduce g forces to less than 1g on passenger aircrafts. 
How do you unload the airplane to less than 1g?
ANSWER: By pushing forward on the pitch controls 
What are the benefits of unloading?
ANSWER: 
Increases the roll rate
Decreases the stall speed

ASK:
What are the three sources of energy?
ANSWER: 
Kinetic energy, which increases with increasing airspeed.
Potential energy, which is proportional to altitude.
Chemical energy, from the fuel in the tanks which can be converted to thrust. 

These three types of energy can be traded, or exchanged:
ANSWER: 
Airspeed can be traded for altitude (kinetic to potential energy)
Altitude can be traded for airspeed (potential to kinetic energy)
Thrust can be converted into airspeed and/or altitude (chemical to either kinetic or potential energy)

slides.n:
SAY:
Data Sources & Methodology
This analysis combines data from multiple authoritative sources:
IATA Loss of Control In-Flight Report (2019) - Comprehensive analysis of 64 LOC-I accidents from 2009-2018
Boeing Statistical Summary (2024) - Annual accident statistics through 2024
NTSB/EASA/Ethiopian Investigation Reports - Official findings on 737 MAX accidents
IATA Annual Safety Report (2024) - Recent accident categorizations
Key Discussion Points
Prevention vs. Recovery: Most LOC-I accidents occur because pilots don’t recognize the developing upset condition early enough
Altitude Matters: 27% occur in initial climb - low altitude means less time for recovery
Training Evolution: Post-737 MAX, emphasis shifted to understanding ALL aircraft systems, not just “differences training”
The Startle Factor: When systems behave unexpectedly, pilot response time and accuracy degrades significantly

SAY: 
UPRT / EET Learning Points include:
Monitor flight path closely—don’t rely solely on automation.

ASK: What is the correct upset recovery sequence?
ANSWER: 
Recognize and confirm the developing situation
Disengage autopilot
Disconnect autothrottle
Recover:
Recover from stall, if needed
Roll in the shortest direction to wings level. If bank angle is more than 90 degrees, unload and roll. *
Complete the recovery:
Apply nose up elevator
Apply nose up trim, if needed *
Adjust thrust and drag, if needed.

Do the 747-400 and -8 have Flight Envelope Protection during manual flight?
ANSWER: 
747-400: NO
747-8: With A/T armed, the A/T automatically activates if no autopilot or F/D active, or an autopilot or F/D is in VNAV PTH, VNAV ALT, ALT, V/S, or G/S, and:
Speed less than an FMC calculated value for one second
Thrust below reference thrust
Airplane altitude above 100 feet RA on approach, or airplane barometric altitude 400 feet above airport on takeoff
FCOM Vol 2 4.20.19
Both: During Autoflight, The automatic flight control system provides stall and overspeed protection. Stall protection prevents speed reduction below the minimum maneuvering speed. Overspeed protection prevents exceeding the maximum operating, gear extended, or flap placard speed. FCOM Vol 2 4.20.17

ASK:
What is the difference between a normal go-around and a go-around after you’ve touched the runway? FCTM 6.19
ANSWER: A balked landing is a discontinued landing attempt and go-around initiated at or after touchdown, but prior to initiation of reverse thrust. The balked landing technique maintains landing flap configuration to expedite climb away from the runway environment. Considerations for a balked landing include clearance of an obstacle in the runway environment, insufficient runway for continued landing, or transitioning to a go-around from a low-energy state. Note: When landing, the TO/GA switches are inhibited near touchdown and on the ground.

When is the TO/GA function inhibited? FCOM NP. 05.1 
ANSWER: TO/GA function is inhibited close to the ground and after touchdown. If the thrust levers do not respond when TO/GA is pushed, or if the go-around is initiated after touchdown, advance the thrust levers manually to go-around thrust.

ASK:
Define a rejected landing, bounced landing, and balked landing. FCTM 1.4
ANSWER: 
A bounced landing is defined as a landing where both main gears contact the ground and then both main gears leave the ground prior to landing. 
A rejected Landing is a discontinued landing attempt and go-around initiated at low altitude (below DA(H) or MDA(H)) but prior to touchdown. If a rejected landing becomes necessary, follow the Go-Around and Missed Approach procedure as prescribed in the FCOM/QRH.
A balked landing is a discontinued landing attempt and go-around initiated at or after touchdown, but prior to initiation of reverse thrust, when the airplane is in a low-energy state with thrust at or near IDLE and airspeed decreasing below VREF.
How could higher than idle thrust through initial touchdown contribute to a bounced landing? FCTM 6.18
ANSWER: If higher than idle thrust is maintained through initial touchdown, the automatic speedbrake deployment may be disabled even when the speedbrakes are armed. This can result in a bounced landing.
(O) What is the first step recovery? in a bounced landing FCTM 6.18
ANSWER: 
If the airplane bounces during a landing attempt, hold or re-establish a normal landing attitude and add thrust as necessary to control the rate of descent. 
Thrust need not be added for a shallow bounce or skip. 
If a high, hard bounce occurs, initiate a go-arou

ASK:
What is Optimal Eye Position and why is it important? FCTM 2.10 
ANSWER: The pilot must be seated as to see the following during taxi, takeoff and landing: The lower outboard corner of the pilot’s forward window is a good visual reference for the outboard side of the wing gear wheels on the same side. The lower inboard corner of the pilot’s forward window is also a good reference for the opposite side wing gear wheels.
(O) When is it recommended to disengage the autopilot if a manual landing is to be performed? FCTM 6.8
ANSWER: 
Manual flight should be planned early enough to allow the pilot time to establish airplane control before beginning the flare.
It is recommended that the PF should consider disengaging the autopilot and disconnecting the autothrottle no later than 1 to 2 nm before the threshold, or approximately 300 to 600 feet above field elevation.

ANSWER: When the landing environment becomes visible. A gradual transition should begin to outside references and acquiring a visual aim point of reference.

ASK:
What is the objective of training Slow Flight AC120-111
ANSWER: This maneuver demonstrates the low energy or high drag configuration with the slow response to flight control and thrust inputs. This is to enhance the pilot’s knowledge and recognition of the low-speed handling qualities prior to stall training.

What is the difference between Minimum Maneuver Speed vs Flap Maneuver Speed? FCTM 1.16
ANSWER: Minimum maneuver speeds (displayed as the top of the lower amber band) should not be confused with flap maneuver speeds. Flap maneuver speeds are based on airplane weight, while the minimum maneuver speed is calculated using airplane angle of attack and current airspeed. These speeds provide independent means to ensure that the current airspeed provides at least full maneuver capability for terminal-area maneuvering.

Does the stall recovery procedure change based on altitude? FCOM MAN 1.1
ANSWER: No, we only have one stall recovery procedure.

ANSWER: The first indication of a stall approaching is the AIRSPEED LOW EICAS message.
When must we recover from a stall warning? FCTM 7.12 & FCOM MAN1.1
ANSWER: Whichever occurs first:
artificial indication (stick shaker) 
natural indication (initial buffet).
What are the indications of a stall? FCTM 7.12
ANSWER: An airplane stall is characterized by one or more of the following conditions:
stall warning 
artificial (stick shaker) 
natural (buffet which could be heavy at times) or
lack of pitch authority
lack of roll control
inability to arrest descent rate.
What are the steps that must be accomplished at the first indication of a stall (buffet or stick shaker)?
ANSWER: Refer to Approach to Stall image above.
Completing the recovery states “Establish pitch attitude.” This means the buffet and stick shaker have stopped and proper configuration changes have been accomplished per the procedure. What are some approximate pitch attitudes that would be appropriate after recovery for different phases of flight? FCOM NP.35.3, QRH PI.20.5
ANSWER: 
15 degrees after rotation
Approximately 10 degrees terminal climb
Approximately 5 degrees passing 10,000 in route climb 
Approximately 2.5 degrees Level Flight flaps up 
Is a successful stall recovery dependent on re-engaging the autopilot or auto

ASK:
What defines an Unusual Attitude or Upset condition? FCOM MAN.1.14
ANSWER: 
An upset condition is any time an airplane is diverting from the intended airplane state. An airplane upset can involve pitch or roll angle deviations as well as inappropriate airspeeds for the conditions.
Historically, an upset was defined as unintentionally exceeding one or more of the following conditions:
Pitch attitude greater than 25 degrees nose up
Pitch attitude greater than 10 degrees nose down
Bank angle greater than 45 degrees
Less than the above parameters but flying at an airspeed inappropriate for the conditions.
When accomplishing a recovery from aircraft upset what must be accomplished first? FCOM MAN.1.14
ANSWER: If the airplane is stalled, first recover from the stall before accomplishing the upset recovery 
What is the guidance for a Nose High Recovery? FCOM MAN.1.15
ANSWER: Recognize and confirm the developing situation. Then:
Pilot Flying:
Disengage autopilot 
Disconnect autothrottle 
Recover: 
Apply nose down elevator. Apply as much elevator as needed to obtain a nose down pitch rate. 
Apply appropriate nose down stabilizer trim. * 
Reduce thrust 
Roll (adjust bank angle) to obtain a nose down pitch rate. * 
Complete the recovery: 
When approaching the horizon, roll to wings level 
Check airspeed and adjust thrust
Establish pitch attitude
Pilot Monitoring: 
Call out attitude, airspeed and altitude throughout the recovery 
Verify all needed actions have been done and call out
